legacy_report:
SOURCE: "REFRAG: Rethinking RAG based Decoding", Xiaoqiang Lin (first author; work done at Meta, NUS affiliation), Aritra Ghosh, Bryan Kian Hsiang Low, Anshumali Shrivastava, Vijai Mohan. Meta Superintelligence Labs. Preprint, arXiv:2509.01092v2, dated 14 Oct 2025 (cs.CL). No venue stated. Code "will be available" at github.com/facebookresearch/refrag.

COVERAGE: all 30 pages, 106,052 chars extracted. I read the body, the appendices (latency math, RL formulation, ablation tables 11-14, RAG tables 15-17, summarization table 21) and skimmed references. I did not read the 5-passage Bruce Lee text in table 10 or the generated summaries (tables 19/20) in detail. Figure images were not inspected; I only read their captions from the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- REFRAG cuts time-to-first-token (TTFT) sharply by feeding precomputed chunk embeddings instead of passage tokens to the decoder.
  number: 16.53x TTFT with cached chunk embeddings and 8.59x without, at k=16, context 16384; CEPE gets 2.01x and 1.04x. At k=32, 30.85x over LLaMA and 3.75x over CEPE.
  setup: LLaMA-2-7B decoder, RoBERTa-large encoder, batch size 1, single A100, same modelling file and flash-attention for all baselines. Figure 2 plots acceleration against input tokens.
  quote: "REFRAG with k = 16 achieves 16.53× TTFT acceleration with cache and 8.59× without cache1, both surpassing CEPE (2.01× and 1.04×, respectively)"
  where: p3, section 2; appendix A
  Warning: the abstract says 30.85x, the intro says "30.75×", and p3 says "32.99×" for k=32 (appendix: "up to 32.99× acceleration in TTFT"). The source is inconsistent here.
- On equal latency, RAG accuracy improves because the saved tokens buy more passages.
  number: at a strong retriever and up to 10 passages, REFRAG matches LLaMA with 5.26x TTFT speedup. At equal latency (8 passages vs 1), +1.22% average over 16 RAG tasks (strong retriever) and +1.93% (weak retriever). At 10 passages, weak retriever: +0.71% and 5.26x TTFT.
  setup: LLaMA-2-7B fine-tuned on a 1.1M-example QA mix (LLaMA_FT baseline). Retrieval: DRAGON+ over a 400M-passage Wikipedia and CommonCrawl corpus, passages under 200 words. Weak retriever means 200 retrieved and K picked at random. Metrics are exact match, F1 or accuracy by task. REFRAG8 uses the same decoder token count as 1 passage.
  quote: "With a strong retriever and a maximum of 10 passages, REFRAG matches LLaMA's performance while achieving a 5.26× speedup in TTFT. At equal latency (8 passages for REFRAG vs. 1 for LLaMA), REFRAG attains a 1.22% average improvement across 16 RAG tasks."
  where: p8, section 5.1; figure 4
- Theory says compression gives k times the TTFT and throughput gain at short contexts and k^2 times at long contexts. KV cache shrinks by about k.
  number: "k×" short, "k2×" long.
  setup: LLaMA-2-7B, bfloat16, assumes chunk embeddings are precomputed and cached. TTFT is compute-bound, decoding is memory-bound.
  quote: "Theoretical analysis (section A) shows that for short context lengths, our method achieves up to k× acceleration in TTFT and throughput. For longer context length, acceleration reaches up to k2× for both metrics."
  where: p3; appendix table 6 and table 9
- Decoding speed per token (TTIT) barely improves, about 3x at long context. CEPE is slower than plain LLaMA on this measure.
  number: 3x
  quote: "In terms of TTIT, we achieve 3× acceleration in long context scenario in both cached and not cached scenarios."
  where: appendix A
- Perplexity is close to the full-context model at 2048 context.
  number: REFRAG8 Arxiv P2048 1.062 vs LLaMA-Full 1.069, CEPE 1.107, LLaMA256 1.171. REFRAG16 is 9.3% better than CEPE on average log-perplexity. REFRAG32 roughly matches CEPE.
  setup: LLaMA-2-7B, trained on a 20B-token Slimpajama sample (50% Arxiv, 50% Book). Tested on Arxiv, Book, PG19 and ProofPile with s=2048 context and o of 512, 1024 or 2048 output tokens (table 1). Context lengths 4096 to 16384 are in table 2.
  quote: "With a compression rate of 16, we achieve a 9.3% average log-perplexity improvement over CEPE across four datasets"
  where: p5, tables 1 and 2
  The "without loss in perplexity" in the abstract is stronger than table 1 shows. REFRAG16 and REFRAG32 are worse than REFRAG8 and worse than full context. REFRAG matches full context only at k=8.
- Compression lets the context extend past the decoder's native window.
  number: 16x context extension (abstract). Multi-turn: REFRAG beats LLaMA_FT on all three datasets at 10 passages.
  setup: LLaMA-2-7B has a 4k window. Datasets are TopiOCQA, ORConvQA and QReCC. Table 4 and table 5: at 10 passages, TopiOCQA 23.60 for LLaMA_FT vs 27.62 for REFRAG, and ORConvQA 15.72 vs 19.67. At 5 passages LLaMA_FT wins on QReCC.
  where: p8-9
- Selective expansion by an RL policy beats a fixed lower compression rate.
  number: REFRAG16+RL at effective rate 8.25 matches or beats REFRAG8 trained at k=8 (table 13). RL beats the perplexity heuristics and random selection (figure 3).
  setup: policy is a two-layer transformer over chunk embeddings. Trained with GRPO-style updates, reward is negative log-perplexity of the output tokens. Fine-tuned with p=0.1, so 90% of chunks are compressed.
  quote: "Table 13 demonstrates that REFRAG16 with RL-based selective compression consistently outperforms REFRAG8 across different datasets and context lengths."
  where: p6, appendix A.1
- Baselines collapse with 80 passages. The strongest ones are not like-for-like.
  number: with 80 passages, NQ is 0.03 for CEPE_D and 1.24 for LLaMA-32K. REFRAG8 scores 24.15 and LLaMA_FT with 10 passages scores 26.08. REFRAG8 on 80 passages has no clear gain over its own 8-10 passage score.
  where: table 3, p9. Table 15 shows many tasks flat or lower beyond about 20-50 passages (NQ 24.30 at 20, 24.15 at 80).
- Training recipe: curriculum learning and a reconstruction pre-task are essential.
  number: reconstruction log-perplexity at P16 is 0.669 with curriculum vs 3.719 without (table 11). CPT P16 is 2.017 with reconstruction vs 3.272 without (table 12).
  quote: "Counterintuitively, directly continuing pre-training of the decoder to utilize encoder outputs did not reduce perplexity, even for the reconstruction task."
  where: p4, p6, tables 11-12
- Compression has a practical limit.
  number: k=64 "appears to be overly aggressive"; k=32 is still competitive.
  where: p7, figure 10
- Retrieved passages show block-diagonal attention. Within-passage attention is much larger than cross-passage attention.
  setup: one query ("how bruce lee died"), 5 hand-picked dissimilar passages, LLaMA-2-7B-Chat. Qualitative only, with no number.
  where: figure 7, appendix C. It is the motivating evidence, from n=1.
- Summarization at equal decoder tokens favours REFRAG.
  number: at 128 decoder tokens, Arxiv Rouge-1 is 36.50 (REFRAG8) and 38.48 (REFRAG16) vs 29.69 for LLaMA_FT.
  where: table 21, p30
- Larger decoder helps more than a larger encoder, and the recipe transfers to other models.
  number: LLaMA-3.1-8B with RoBERTa-Large at 4096 context gives P2048 0.998, vs 0.972 for full context at 2048.
  where: p7, table 14

LIMITS
- Needs training. A continual-pretraining stage (20B tokens, 8 nodes x 8 H100), SFT and an RL policy, plus a projection layer. It is not a drop-in for an API model. "Without modifications to the LLM architecture" refers to the decoder, with an added encoder.
- The headline speedup figures come from a single A100, batch size 1, LLaMA-2-7B. They do not show serving behaviour under batching or on other models. The cached numbers assume chunk embeddings are precomputed and stored. The cache storage cost is not quantified.
- Quality is measured mainly by perplexity. The RAG task gains are small (1-2%) and come from a task-mix fine-tune. Text-answer faithfulness and citation quality are not tested. The paper concedes the retriever setting is simulated (weak retriever means random picks from 200).
- Table 16 (equal context of 5 passages) shows no model clearly dominates. The text says "no model significantly outperforms others". The speedup is the gain at equal accuracy.
- Exact match is stricter than in other work, so absolute numbers are lower than elsewhere (footnote 3).
- The paper offers no real discussion of limitations. The only stated limit is the compression ceiling (k=64).
- Code was not released at v2. Models are LLaMA-2 era.

BUILDS ON
- CEPE (Yen et al., 2024): the main baseline, and the source of the next-paragraph-prediction CPT method.
- REPLUG (Shi et al., 2024).
- Fusion-in-decoder (Izacard and Grave, 2021).
- RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022).
- Compressive transformer (Rae et al., 2020).
- Chevalier et al., 2023 (AutoCompressors).
- Prompt compression: LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023), LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024), Selective Context. Stated as "complementary".
- RA-DIT-style fine-tune data (Lin et al., 2024).
- RL: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), Pointer Networks masking and combinatorial RL (Bello et al., 2017; Dai et al., 2017).
- Latency model: Liu et al., 2025.
- DRAGON+ retriever (Lin et al., 2023).
- Also cited: Kuratov et al., 2025; PCC (Dai et al., 2025).

CODE: none in the paper. The useful formulas are in appendix B.4 (p20-21). Prefill is compute-bound, with latency (24d^2+4ds)lbs/f. Decode is memory-bound, with latency (2n+4dlb(s+o))/m. KV cache is 4dlb(s+o) before and 4dlb(s/k+o) after.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p3): architecture. Context chunked, encoded by a light encoder, projected into decoder token space, RL policy picks chunks to expand. Best single picture of the idea.
- Fig 2 (p3): TTFT, TTIT and throughput acceleration against input tokens at k=16, cached vs not cached vs CEPE. Figures 8 (k=32) and 9 (k=8) are in the appendix.
- Fig 3 (p6): log-perplexity against compression rate for RL, perplexity heuristics and random selection.
- Fig 4 (p7): RAG performance against number of passages and against latency, strong and weak retriever.
- Fig 7 (p22): block-diagonal cross-passage attention heatmaps, all 32 layers.
- Table 6 (p16): symbolic table of k and k^2 gains.

PROBLEMS: no embedded instructions. The text extraction of tables is mixed together (bolding removed, numbers run together). The 30.75x, 30.85x and 32.99x inconsistency noted above. The first-page abstract extract is missing some text, so I cut the quote. Figures were not viewed.

NOTE CHECK
- Grep of notes/06-generation-for-rag.md, notes/07-rag-in-production.md and references.md finds no mention of REFRAG, CEPE, chunk embedding or KV cache. The only related content is the LLMLingua row at notes/06 line 242 (section "Order and size of the context", about prompt compression) and the references.md LLMLingua row. The Latency table at notes/07 lines 327-338 lists levers (router, smaller or quantized LLM, caching, dropping components) but nothing about prefill cost or input compression.
- The strongest point bears on notes/07 "Latency" (TTFT is quadratic in prompt length and RAG contexts are mostly passages with block-diagonal attention, so compressing them cuts first-token latency). A second place is notes/06 "Order and size of the context", next to LLMLingua as a trained embedding-level alternative to token-level compression. notes/06 line 151 only mentions "Time to first token and tokens per second" as a model-selection metric. The notes do not already say it, so this is a new row, not a "sharpens".
- Caveat for the writer: REFRAG requires training and a custom decoder, so it can't be applied to hosted APIs. Put it as a research direction with the 8.59x or 16.53x (k=16, 16k context, one A100, LLaMA-2-7B) figure and its setup, not as a production lever.
